summary:
The Congenital Heart Futures Reauthorization Act of 2024 (Pub. L. 118-107) amends Section 399V-2 of the Public Health Service Act (42 U.S.C. § 280g-13) to reauthorize and expand the national congenital heart disease research, surveillance, and awareness program. 

The Act contains two primary operative mechanisms. First, it extends the program’s funding authorization period. Section 2(3) of the Act amends redesignated subsection (h) of 42 U.S.C. § 280g-13 to strike the authorization of appropriations for fiscal years 2020 through 2024 and insert an authorization of appropriations for fiscal years 2025 through 2029. 

Second, Section 2(1) and 2(2) of the Act establish new reporting and strategic planning mandates. The Act redesignates existing subsections (f) and (g) as (g) and (h), respectively, and inserts a new subsection (f), titled "Report and Strategy." Under paragraph (1) of the new subsection, the Secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS) is required to submit a report to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions within two years of the Act's enactment (November 21, 2024). This report must describe past and present HHS activities to increase public awareness and provider education regarding congenital heart disease, specifically addressing patients' lifelong needs, and must assess the current domestic workforce capacity of healthcare providers treating adult congenital heart disease patients.

Under paragraph (2) of the new subsection, the Secretary is mandated to develop and submit to Congress a strategic plan within one year of submitting the initial report. The strategy must outline methods to improve public awareness, provider education, and training. It must include findings and recommendations to address research and awareness gaps regarding lifelong patient needs (including long-term outcomes, quality of life, mental health, and healthcare utilization), mitigate workforce shortages in adult congenital heart disease care (including enhancing fellowship or continuing education programs), and foster interagency and stakeholder collaboration. In developing this strategy, the Secretary is directed to consult with qualified stakeholders, including patient organizations, healthcare professionals, research entities, health insurance providers, accrediting organizations, and relevant Federal agencies, specifically naming the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the National Institutes of Health, and the Health Resources and Services Administration.
